hazard_statements: H224 Extremely flammable liquid and vapour
H336 May cause drowsiness or dizziness

sds_facts.storage: Keep container tightly closed in a dry and well- ventilated place. Keep away from heat and sources of ignition.

bench_knowledge.because: High vapor pressure (≥5 kPa at 20°C) causes significant evaporation inside the tip. Without pre-wetting, the headspace is dry air; the solvent flash-evaporates into it, creating a vapour cushion that compresses and releases unpredictably, drifting dispensed volume by 5–15%. Three aspirate-expel cycles saturate the headspace before the actual dispensing step. Fast dispense minimises dwell-time in the tip.
bench_knowledge.cite: Eppendorf Application Note: Pipetting Volatile Liquids, 2018. NIST WebBook CAS 64-17-5 (vapor pressure 5.95 kPa at 20°C).

bench_knowledge.because: Light-sensitive reagents degrade under UV or visible light by different mechanisms depending on the compound class. Fluorophores (DAPI, ethidium bromide) undergo irreversible photobleaching — the chromophore is destroyed; 30 seconds of UV transilluminator exposure causes measurable DAPI signal loss. Oxidizers (H₂O₂, NaOCl) photodecompose, losing titer. Peroxide-forming solvents (diethyl ether) form hydroperoxides faster in light. Light-activated monomers (acrylamide) can begin polymerising spontaneously. Amber containers or foil-wrap block the relevant wavelengths for all of these.
bench_knowledge.cite: Thermo Fisher Scientific: DAPI Technical Data Sheet (D1306). Lakowicz, Principles of Fluorescence Spectroscopy, 3rd ed., Ch. 1. Sigma-Aldrich H₂O₂ Product Information (216763).

bench_knowledge.because: Volatile peroxide-forming solvents such as diethyl ether, THF, and dioxane form shock-sensitive hydroperoxides on exposure to air and light via autoxidation. Peroxide concentration increases with time and is highest in the last few millilitres as the solvent evaporates. Opening a bottle without a peroxide test when the contents are old or unknown is a documented explosion hazard. Max 3-month working life after opening; test with commercial peroxide strips before each use; discard at 25 ppm peroxide or above. Less volatile, weaker peroxide formers need separate class-specific rules rather than this strict ether-style handling rule.
bench_knowledge.cite: Jackson HL et al. (1998) Chem Health Safety 5(3): 16–18 (ether peroxide hazards). Prudent Practices in the Laboratory, NRC 2011, Ch. 6.

bench_knowledge.because: The SDS (Section 7 or 8) specifies ventilation controls or fume hood use for this reagent. This category spans volatile toxic solvents (pyridine, DMF, heptane), cytotoxic and genotoxic compounds (docetaxel, streptozocin, azoxymethane), and reagents whose vapours or aerosols pose an inhalation hazard. A chemical fume hood provides the primary engineering control — never handle these reagents on the open bench.
bench_knowledge.cite: OSHA Laboratory Standard 29 CFR 1910.1450. Manufacturer SDS Section 7/8.

bench_knowledge.because: Flammable liquids (flash point < 60°C) generate ignitable vapours at or near room temperature. NFPA 30 and OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 require storage in FM-approved flammable liquid storage cabinets whenever quantities exceed the exempt amount in standard laboratory containers. Class IB/IC solvents (heptane fp −4°C, ethyl acetate fp −4°C, pyridine fp 20°C) have vapour densities > 1 and will pool at floor level near ignition sources such as hot plates and electrical outlets. Hood use is governed by volatility, toxicity, open-container volume, and SDS ventilation language; the flammable flag alone is enough to require storage and ignition-source controls, but not enough to make every small transfer a hood-only operation.
bench_knowledge.cite: NFPA 30: Flammable and Combustible Liquids Code (2021). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 (flammable liquids storage).

bench_knowledge.because: Volatile flammable liquids can generate ignitable vapour concentrations during open-container transfer, especially when the vapour is heavier than air or the operation involves more than brief capped-vial handling. Use a chemical fume hood or equivalent local exhaust for open transfers to keep vapour below hazardous concentrations and away from ignition sources.
bench_knowledge.cite: Prudent Practices in the Laboratory, NRC 2011, Ch. 6.C and 9.C. NFPA 30: Flammable and Combustible Liquids Code (2021).
